stimulus.text: The resistance to British taxes was not only the work of famous leaders. In 1774, fifty-one women in Edenton, North Carolina, signed a declaration vowing to give up tea and other British products. Across the colonies, women organized spinning bees to make homespun cloth, replacing British imports. In Boston, shoemaker Ebenezer Macintosh led crowd actions against Stamp Act officials, and artisans who backed the boycotts found new demand for American-made goods.

books.section: B. The Resistance Movement from Above and from Below

stem: The spinning bees and homespun cloth described in the passage served which of the following purposes?

options.text: They raised money to pay the Stamp Act tax
options.misconception: Homespun cloth was not sold to pay the tax — it replaced British cloth so colonists could boycott British goods without going without.

options.text: They provided uniforms for the Continental Army
options.misconception: The Continental Army did not exist until 1775, and the spinning bees of the 1760s and 1770s made household cloth for the boycott, not military uniforms.

options.text: They proved that colonial women supported British rule
options.misconception: The spinning bees were acts of resistance, not loyalty — the women spun to replace British goods, which is the opposite of supporting British rule.

options.text: They let colonists boycott British goods while still clothing themselves

rationales.D: Background: a boycott fails if people cannot live without the boycotted goods. Spinning bees made homespun cloth at home, so families could refuse British imports and still have clothes to wear — resistance you could put on.
rationales.A: No money was raised for the tax. Homespun replaced British cloth; it did not pay Parliament.
rationales.B: There was no Continental Army in the 1760s. The cloth was for households, not for soldiers.
rationales.C: Spinning was resistance, not loyalty. The women spun precisely to stop buying British goods.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what a boycott needs to survive. An alternative: people must be able to live without the goods they refuse.
2. Ask what homespun provided. Cloth made at home, by the women who otherwise bought British textiles.
3. See the double purpose. The spinning bee was both practical and political — it clothed families and it advertised resistance, since homespun became a visible badge of the cause.
Remember: the best protest is one you can live with — find the alternative that makes refusal possible.
